Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Cellular and Circuit Organization of the Locus Coeruleus of Adult Mice" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 2 peer reviewers, and the evaluation has been overseen by a Reviewing Editor and John Huguenard as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in the review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Nelson Totah (Reviewer #1).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

Essential revisions:

1) Based on their findings, the authors argue that locus coeruleus noradrenaline neurons do not communicate through direct, excitatory synaptic transmission. However, this possibility has not been ruled out through their experiments as the horizontal slice preparation likely severed some axonal connections. The authors could try performing some experiments in coronal slices in which axonal connectivity may be somewhat more spared. Alternatively, they could moderate their claims in this aspect of the study.

2) The authors also argue that their results support the idea that lateral inhibition through alpha2 adrenergic receptors does not occur in the LC. However, there is a wealth of data supporting the existence of lateral inhibition and the present finding are based on the stimulation of single LC-noradrenaline neurons without a more parametric analysis of different stimulation frequencies/timing. For example, it is possible, given that LC neurons often fire together, that the activity of many LC neurons at one time is required to detect lateral inhibition, as noted by the authors in the discussion. In addition, given previous work showing that the frequency and timing of spikes are important in producing and detecting lateral inhibition (see Rev. 2 comments below and Huang et al. 2007. Proc National Acad Sci 104, 1401-1406), further exploration of this question is warranted. The authors could attempt stimulation of multiple LC-noradrenergic neurons at one time (possibly using optogenetic approaches) and/or explore the parametric space more extensively. Alternatively, they could remove this section from the paper.

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

Congratulations to the authors on an extremely difficult set of experiments, stunning anatomy, and careful analyses to address important and timely questions about the LC. Really (to my knowledge) no one has dug into the anatomy like this since a few Japanese groups in 1978/1979 and Americans in mid-1980's. An update was needed – and to couple them with recordings is a truly unique data set. I have some comments and questions which I hope will help the authors to improve the manuscript and connect it better with the existing literature.

One of the major strengths of the Author's work is the ability to potentially connect LC neuron types (FF and MP) with the two types of previously reported extracellular single unit. In light of that, additional characterization of a few things would be help to the field in making the connection to single units. The authors show clear data that FF cells may correspond to 'narrow units' because they have narrow AP width and have larger (albeit not significantly) AHP. Do FF have higher FR as do "narrow units"? Where were the FF neurons located in the LC core? The "narrow units" have been shown to be located throughout the core, but biased ventrally. This info would help link to existing extracellular study identifying multiple cell types.

It is a bit strange that Figure 1C and 1D come after Figure 2. It may improve the flow of the manuscript to move those panels into figure 2.

Figure 2E – it would be helpful to have a conceptual description of what it would mean to be low x value – low y value versus high x value – high y value.

Figure 2F – are the rings here the number of neurons? It would be helpful to the reader if the authors could label the axis and state this in the legend.

Figure 2H, 2I – it would help to explain that Y axis of panel is related to branching point. It is not clear to me how to interpret this plot. it might be standard in this field but would help the general reader to have this information briefly in the Results section or figure legend to better understand the plot.

Figure 3A ("Cell 7 and Cell 2 is electrically coupled") – "is" should be "are".

Figure 7C – This plot in C is confusing. The methods state that a horizontal (transverse) plane was used, therefore, ventral and dorsal should be medial and lateral. Can the Authors clarify this?

Line 78 – strike "the".

Line 94 – Can the authors comment on Why the RMP is so different from what was reported in earlier work (see Supplementary Table 5 in Chandler, Gao, and Waterhouse. 2014. Proc National Acad Sci 111, 6816-682)?

Lines 132-134 – The fact that the axon originated from different locations on FF versus MP cells is interesting. Is this common in other brain regions and various cell types? How does this affect spike generation and spike conductance based on axonal location? This could be useful to briefly discuss, but this comment is not a criticism or request for necessary information. This is just a curious question and something could be added only if the authors see how answering it could be beneficial to understanding LC-NE release and noradrenergic neuromodulation.

Lines 145-148 – Given that there was a sampling bias with some slices heavily enriched with FF and other slices with MP, can the authors say the dorsal-ventral levels of the FF sample biased slices? I understood that horizontal/transverse slicing was used, so some slices were more ventral than others. Were surrounding slices stained to enable precise knowledge of the location in the dorsal-ventral axis? Prior work showed that single units of narrow type were biased to be more ventral (Totah, et al. 2018. Neuron 99, 1055-1068.e6) and ventrally distributed narrow waveform units have been shown to have distinct functional roles (Li, et al. 2016. Brain Res 1641, 274-290; Hirschberg, et al. 2017. eLife 6, e29808). Thus, showing that FF units are also ventrally biased would help link the present work with extracellular work.

Line 204 – Given the importance of the present study in linking with extracellular recordings used in functional/behavioral studies of LC, it may be noted that Totah, et al. 2018. Neuron 99, 1055-1068.e6 found that 6% of all unit pairs had a CC consistent with a gap injection, which is very similar to the 4.3% that the authors report.

Line 209 – Do the authors mean Figure 4D instead of 4A?

Lines 220-221 – The authors may wish to note that their results are consistent with the extracellular study of CC's reporting putative gap junction mediated interactions in adult rat (Totah et al. 2018), intracellular recordings showing gap junction blockade dependent Vm coupling (Alvarez, et al. 2002. Proc National Acad Sci 99, 4032-4036), as well as anatomical studies showing gap junctions are present in adult rat LC (Bockstaele, et al. 2004. Neurochem Int 45, 421-428; Rash, J. E. et al. 2007. Neuroscience 147, 938-956).

Lines 190 – 225 – without the use of a gap junction blocker, it should be made clear that the electrical coupling is likely or putatively gap junction mediated.

Lines 411 – 414 – The description of prior work is a bit unclear when using the terms "dorsal horn" and "ventral horn" given that there is an anterior horn (which lies largely dorsal to the LC core) and a posterior horn. It would be helpful to clarify this. My understanding of Loughlin et al. 1986 is that they found: large MP cells in the ventromedial aspect of the LC core (consistent with later work by Hirschberg et al. and Li et al) and in the anterior horn of the LC (which is by definition at the dorsal edge of the LC core or even more dorsal than LC core); medium size MP cells throughout the LC core; and FF cells that were strongly anterior-posterior oriented and located on the dorsal edge of the LC core.

Loughlin also observed "small, round cells" which might be similar to the "oval" cells reported by Shimizu et al. (SHIMIZU, N., OHNISHI, S., SATOH, K. and TOHYAMA, M. 1978. Cellular Organization of Locus Coeruleus in the Rat as Studied by Golgi Method. Arch Histol Japon 41, 103-112). Did the authors happen to observe these?

Lines 496 – 499 – the finding of FF and MP specific networks of electrically coupled cells links nicely with the finding that LC pairwise correlated firing identified in extracellular recordings are cell-type specific (Totah, et al. 2018. Neuron 99, 1055-1068.e6), as are LC ensembles (Noei, et al. 2022. Proc National Acad Sci 119, e2116507119). This again is an important point because the present work serves to build a bridge between cell morphology and membrane characteristics with extracellular recordings of different unit types performed in functional/behavioral studies (Hirschberg, et al. 2017. eLife 6, e29808; Breton-Provencher, et al. 2022. Nature 1-7 doi:10.1038/s41586-022-04782-2).

The work is overall abbreviation heavy and the authors could write out ISD, EC, and CC instead of abbreviating them.

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

I do not think there is sufficient evidence presented here to reject the notion that local NE is released and perhaps affects LC function. Although the authors take two different current injection approaches (resulting in 1 AP or 5 AP), we simply do not know where to sample to determine if NE is playing a role. Two explanation seems just as plausible as 'no chemical transmission'. (1) The multipatch approach could just not have neurons that receive NE from the upstream neurons. (2) Even 5 AP may not release NE in a manner that would physiologically activate alpha2-AR. In this prep does blockade of alpha2 depolarize the cells? That would suggest tonic alpha2 activity that the addition of 1 or 5 APs would perhaps not elevate to the point of observation. As it stands, I would be more comfortable with the stated conclusion being that no fast-acting small molecule transmission (i.e. glutamate) was observed, rather than ruling out all chemical transmission.

Prior to eliminating the possibility of local chemical transmission entirely, it might well be worth performing this approach in coronal slices where peri-LC glutamate transmission is better maintained and the cells still firing phasically.

While the authors describe the imaging-based synapses as putative in some instances, these claims should be considered putative in every instance. Without EM or some other synaptic marker, calling these 'synapses' without the putative adjective likely exceeds what can be claimed. I would encourage the authors to ensure these limitations are clear across figures, legends, and each instance in the text. Of course, EM or other markers could be added, but that is not necessary to reach appropriately cautious conclusions.

The claims of 'high quality' and 'sufficiently healthy' LC slices should be operationally defined. What constitutes sufficiency here? Was that the real barrier to multipatch or was it more of a lack of technical and physical expertise?

Why is the n=30 on all cells that were spontaneously active? Shouldn't that number be in the 100s? Is it because the rest of the cells were hyperpolarized to prevent firing? Was there evidence of firing prior to hyperpolarization in those cells? My concern arises from the claim that 'all cells' were active when this was apparently only assayed in 30 of the ~1500 cells.

It appears there is a plotting error in Figure 4 where the trace from C8 is connected to the adjacent cell.

In the discussion, the mention of intersectional approaches should likely be expanded slightly so the meaning is clear. This section would also benefit from citing the relevant work in the LC using these approaches.

Rather than contrasting to 'classical' neurons, I think it would be more appropriate to be specific in the comparison. In other words, from hippocampal neurons rather than classical.

A few LC cell subtypes have already been established (e.g. galanin, NPY, GABA, etc.). Is it possible that either FF or MP cells align with one of these known molecular subtypes?

claims.claim: The LC sends widespread noradrenergic projections to all major divisions of the central nervous system (CNS).
claims.source: The locus coeruleus (LC) is a small pontine nucleus that houses the vast majority of norepinephrine (NE)-producing neurons in the brain and sends widespread noradrenergic projections to all major divisions of the central nervous system (CNS) (Schwarz and Luo, 2015).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: LC dysregulation is implicated in various neuropsychiatric conditions, including depression, anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder.
claims.source: By releasing NE across the CNS, the LC participates in many cognitive processes and behaviors crucial for survival, including fight and flight response, attentional control, and sleep/wake cycles, while its dysregulation is implicated in various neuropsychiatric conditions, including depression, anxiety, autism spectrum disorder, and post-traumatic stress disorder (Bast et al., 2018; Fortress et al., 2015; Southwick et al., 1999; Weinshenker, 2018).
claims.evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claims.claim: LC/NE neurons are heterogeneous in terms of anatomical projections, morpho-electric profiles, and specific behavioral functions.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: The LC is composed of multiple specialized noradrenergic modules with nonoverlapping LC/NE neurons with specific electrophysiological properties and projection targets.
claims.source: Particularly, recent tracing studies coupled with behavioral paradigms suggest that the LC is composed of multiple specialized noradrenergic modules. Each module comprises nonoverlapping LC/NE neurons with specific electrophysiological properties and projection targets, thus participating in distinct functions of the circuits within its efferent domain (Chandler et al., 2014; Li et al., 2016; Totah et al., 2019; Uematsu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: LC/NE neurons within each module are able to switch from a discrete, patterned coding mode to a global broadcast mode to cope with more demanding situations.
claims.source: Interestingly, LC/NE neurons within each module are also able to switch from a discrete, patterned coding mode to a global broadcast mode to cope with the more demanding situation (Uematsu et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior research.

claims.claim: Monoamine neurons, including LC/NE neurons, could co-release glutamate to engage in fast neurotransmission.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.source: However, gap junctions among LC/NE neurons appear to be prevalent only in neonates and decline significantly with age (Christie and Jelinek, 1993; Christie et al., 1989; Travagli et al., 1995).
claims.evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claims.claim: LC/NE neurons at rest had a highly depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP, –43.0 ± 0.1 mV, n=289).
claims.source: LC/NE neurons at rest had a highly depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP, –43.0 ± 0.1 mV, n=289), and all neurons were spontaneously active at rest (1.6 ± 0.4 Hz, n=30; Figure 1B), similar to previous reports on LC neurons (Andrzejewski et al., 2001; Ballantyne et al., 2004; Kuo et al., 2020), but different from hippocampal neurons (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: All LC/NE neurons were spontaneously active at rest (1.6 ± 0.4 Hz, n=30).
claims.source: LC/NE neurons at rest had a highly depolarized resting membrane potential (RMP, –43.0 ± 0.1 mV, n=289), and all neurons were spontaneously active at rest (1.6 ± 0.4 Hz, n=30; Figure 1B), similar to previous reports on LC neurons (Andrzejewski et al., 2001; Ballantyne et al., 2004; Kuo et al., 2020), but different from hippocampal neurons (Figure 1B).

claims.claim: LC/NE neurons were charged much more slowly with a higher input resistance compared to both types of hippocampal neurons in response to negative current injection.

claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing LC neurons to hippocampal neurons, shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: The majority of LC/NE neurons exhibited a characteristic pause after their first action potentials (APs) followed by a series of APs in response to prolonged suprathreshold positive current injection.

claims.evidence: This is based on experimental observations shown in Figure 1C.

claims.claim: LC/NE neurons had much wider action potentials with a lower amplitude, followed by a deep and prolonged afterhyperpolarization compared to hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: LC/NE neurons were also unique in their single APs, which were much wider with a lower amplitude, followed by a deep and prolonged afterhyperpolarization compared to hippocampal neurons (Figure 1C and D).
claims.evidence: This is based on experimental data comparing action potential properties, shown in Figures 1C and 1D.

claims.claim: t-SNE-based clustering approach clearly separated LC neurons from the two types of hippocampal neurons.
claims.source: To illustrate strikingly distinct properties of LC/NE neurons, we extracted 13 electrophysiological features from three groups of neurons (see 'Materials and methods') and plotted them in a t-SNE-map. This t-SNE-based clustering approach clearly separated LC neurons from the two types of hippocampal neurons (Figure 1D), highlighting the unique electrophysiological properties of LC neurons.
claims.evidence: This is based on computational analysis of electrophysiological features, shown in Figure 1D.

claims.claim: Most LC neurons were large cells with smooth dendrites (aspiny), similar to CA1-PVs in the hippocampus, but different from CA1-PCs with spiny dendrites.
claims.source: Most LC neurons were large cells with smooth dendrites (aspiny), similar to CA1-PVs in the hippocampus, but different from CA1-PCs with spiny dendrites (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).

claims.claim: LC/NE neurons had more tortuous dendritic trees with less branch order than hippocampal neurons.

claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: LC/NE neurons could be grouped into two major types: fusiform cells (FF) and multipolar cells (MP).
claims.source: LC/NE neurons had diverse somatodendritic shapes, based on which we could group them into two major types: fusiform cells (FF) and multipolar cells (MP) following previous nomenclature (Swanson, 1976).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis and supported by citation to prior nomenclature.

claims.claim: FFs had an elongated, usually spindle-shaped large soma with two, or rarely three, primary dendrites originating from opposite poles of the soma.
claims.source: FFs had an elongated, usually spindle-shaped large soma with two, or rarely three, primary dendrites originating from opposite poles of the soma (Figure 2C, D and F).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological observations shown in Figures 2C, D, and F.

claims.claim: MP had a triangular or nearly round soma with more than three primary dendrites that could originate from any side of their soma.

claims.evidence: This is based on morphological observations shown in Figures 2A, B, and F.

claims.claim: The dendrites of MPs branched more profusely around the soma compared to that of FF.
claims.source: The dendrites of MPs also branched more profusely around the soma compared to that of FF (Figure 2A, B and G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figures 2A, B, G, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Two types of neurons were well separated in a plot of soma bipolarity against bipolarity index of dendritic arborization.
claims.source: To support LC neuron classification, we reconstructed a subset of LC/NE neurons and quantified their soma bipolarity (i.e., the ratio of the major to the minor axis of a fitted ellipse of the soma; the larger the ratio, the more bipolarity the soma exhibits) and the bipolarity index of dendritic arborization (the proportion of the dendrites originating around the major axis of the fitted ellipse; the larger the proportion, the more bipolarity the dendritic arborizations exhibits) (Figure 2E), and then plotted these two parameters against each other. Two types of neurons were well separated in this plot (Figure 2E).
claims.evidence: This is based on quantitative morphological analysis shown in Figure 2E.

claims.claim: A nonlinear neural network-based classifier could separate two types with a performance accuracy of 100%.
claims.source: We also trained a nonlinear neural network-based classifier to distinguish cell types and the classifier could separate two types with a performance accuracy of 100% (Figure 2—figure supplement 3C).
claims.evidence: This is based on machine learning analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3C.

claims.claim: Soma shape is a reliable criterion to distinguish two types of neurons.
claims.source: Of note, the performance using soma shape alone was almost as good as the performance using two parameters (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B), suggesting that soma shape is a reliable criterion to distinguish two types of neurons.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from machine learning analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B.

claims.claim: Most MPs had their axon originating from the soma (~80%, 37 out of 46 reconstructed MPs).
claims.source: FFs generally had the axon originating from one of the primary dendrites (~95%, 37 out of 39 reconstructed FF neurons, Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2B), suggesting that most FFs have privileged dendrites (i.e., synapses made on these axon-bearing dendrites are in an electrotonically privileged position in evoking action potentials)(Häusser et al., 1995), while most MPs had their axon originating from the soma (~80%, 37 out of 46 reconstructed MPs; Figure 2B, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological observations from 46 reconstructed MPs, shown in Figure 2B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claims.claim: MPs had less local axonal arborization as compared to FFs.
claims.source: In addition, MPs had less local axonal arborization as compared to FFs (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The axon in many MPs had the first branching point located >400 µm away from their origin.
claims.source: The axon in many MPs had the first branching point located >400 µm away from their origin, while the axon in FFs branched much earlier and formed denser local axonal arborization than MPs (Figure 2G, Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: This is based on morphological analysis shown in Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: FFs were not evenly distributed across the entire LC, but preferentially localized in certain anatomical positions.
claims.source: Given that FFs constitute ~38% of total LC/NE neurons, the proportion of FFs in each multicell recording set (the cohort of >3 LCs neurons from each slice) should fall most frequently within the range of 30–40% if FFs are evenly distributed across the entire LC. However, this was not the case in the histogram of FF proportion (Figure 2—figure supplement 4) across all recording sets. Instead, the FF proportions were heavily biased toward either the range of 0–20% or of 50–100%, suggesting that FFs were not evenly distributed across the entire LC, but preferentially localized in certain anatomical positions.

claims.claim: FFs had a narrower spike with a larger amplitude than MPs.

claims.claim: No single excitatory synaptic connection was detected among tested LC neuron pairs.

claims.claim: Sparse electrical connections were identified among LC/NE neurons at the adult stage.

claims.claim: The conductance of putative gap junctions between LC/NE neurons was largely nonrectifying.

results.result: The locus coeruleus (LC) houses the majority of noradrenergic neurons in the brain, sends widespread projections to all major CNS divisions, regulates fundamental functions including fight/flight response, attention control, and sleep/wake cycles, and its dysregulation is implicated in various neuropsychiatric conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C2, C10, and C11 are well-established facts about LC function supported by extensive prior research and multiple citations. These represent foundational background knowledge that is not disputed in the field.

results.result: LC/NE neurons are heterogeneous in terms of anatomical projections, morpho-electric profiles, and behavioral functions, with the LC composed of multiple specialized noradrenergic modules that can switch between discrete coding and global broadcast modes.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C14 are supported by multiple citations to prior research establishing LC heterogeneity and modular organization. This represents established prior work that motivates the current study.

results.result: The NMDG-based slicing protocol enabled preparation of brainstem slices from adult mice containing numerous healthy LC neurons, allowing simultaneous patch-clamp recordings of up to eight mature LC neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C18-C19 describe the methodological achievement demonstrated in Figure 1A and supported by citations to the slicing protocol. This technical advance is critical for the study but represents a methodological contribution rather than a primary finding.

results.result: LC/NE neurons exhibit unique electrophysiological properties distinct from hippocampal neurons, including highly depolarized resting membrane potential (-43.0 ± 0.1 mV), spontaneous activity at rest (1.6 ± 0.4 Hz), slower charging with higher input resistance, characteristic pause after first action potentials, and wider action potentials with lower amplitude followed by deep afterhyperpolarization.
results.evaluation: Claims C20-C25 are supported by experimental measurements from 289 neurons (C20) and 30 neurons (C21), with data shown in Figures 1B-D. The t-SNE clustering analysis (C25) clearly separates LC neurons from hippocampal neurons, validating the distinct electrophysiological profile.

results.result: LC/NE neurons can be classified into two major morphological types based on somatodendritic shape: fusiform cells (FF) with elongated spindle-shaped soma and 2-3 primary dendrites from opposite poles, and multipolar cells (MP) with triangular/round soma and >3 primary dendrites from any side, with MPs having more profusely branching dendrites around the soma.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C34 are supported by morphological analysis shown in Figure 2, quantitative measurements of soma bipolarity and dendritic arborization (C32), and machine learning classification achieving 100% accuracy (C33). The classification is validated by multiple independent approaches and is well-supported by the data.

results.result: FFs and MPs differ in axonal organization: most MPs (~80%) have axons originating from the soma with less local axonal arborization and first branching point >400 µm from origin, while most FFs (~95%) have axons originating from primary dendrites with earlier branching and denser local arborization.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are based on morphological observations from 46 reconstructed MPs and 39 reconstructed FFs, shown in Figures 2B, D, G and Figure 2—figure supplements. The sample sizes are adequate and the differences are clearly documented.

results.result: FFs constitute ~38% (250/666) and MPs ~62% (416/666) of total LC/NE neurons, with FFs not evenly distributed across the LC but preferentially localized in certain anatomical positions as evidenced by bimodal distribution of FF proportions across recording sets.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are based on counting 666 recovered neurons and statistical analysis of FF proportions across recording sets (Figure 2—figure supplement 4). The inference about spatial clustering (C41) is well-supported by the bimodal distribution pattern.

results.result: FFs and MPs exhibit distinct electrophysiological properties: FFs have narrower spikes with larger amplitude, different temporal dynamics, and can sustain higher frequency firing with large suprathreshold depolarizing current injections compared to MPs.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by electrophysiological measurements comparing FF (n=19-39) and MP (n=37-41) shown in Figures 2H-I and Figure 2—source data 1. Statistical significance is reported (p<0.01-0.05) for the differences.

results.result: No excitatory synaptic connections or α2AR-mediated hyperpolarization were detected among more than 1500 tested LC neuron pairs, despite prominent spontaneous EPSPs present in potential postsynaptic neurons.
results.evaluation: Claims C45-C47 are based on systematic testing of >1500 cell pairs with inter-soma distance <150 µm (Figure 3C-D). The negative result is convincing given the large sample size and presence of spontaneous EPSPs confirming cell viability. However, the authors appropriately note this may be preparation-specific.

results.result: Sparse electrical connections were identified among adult LC/NE neurons, with 65 of 1503 tested pairs (4.3%) electrically coupled across inter-soma distances of 16-531 µm, showing bidirectional symmetric coupling with average steady-state coupling coefficient of 0.040±0.028 and largely nonrectifying conductance.
results.evaluation: Claims C48-C52 are supported by experimental data from 1503 tested pairs (Figures 3D, 4C-D, F, I). The coupling coefficient measurements (n=65 coupled pairs) and statistical analysis (slope=1.03, p=0.8) support the nonrectifying nature of gap junctions.

results.result: Electrical coupling rate between LC neurons is distance-dependent, with ~12% coupling rate for inter-soma distance <40 µm that drops quickly as distance increases from 40 µm, though remains relatively constant from 40-240 µm before dropping to zero.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C54 are supported by analysis of coupling rate as a function of inter-soma distance shown in Figure 4E. The biphasic distance dependence with a second small peak around 140 µm is an interesting observation, though the mechanism is not explained.

results.result: The electrical coupling rate in juvenile mice (PND 13-21) was 4.8% (8/165), very similar to adults (4.3%), with no significant difference between ages even when controlling for inter-soma distance, indicating electrical coupling in LC may be less subject to developmental change than previously thought.
results.evaluation: Claims C55 and C120 are supported by experimental data comparing adult and juvenile mice (Figure 4F). This contradicts prior literature (C17, C115, C119) suggesting age-dependent decline. The sample size for juveniles (n=165 pairs) is adequate, though smaller than adults (n=1503).

results.result: Electrical connections in LC neurons are cell-type specific: 8.7% of FF-FF pairs and 5.3% of MP-MP pairs were coupled, while only 0.8% of FF-MP pairs were coupled (p<0.0001). For inter-soma distance <40 µm, FF-FF coupling rate was 31.4% (11/35), MP-MP was 10.7% (7/65), and FF-MP was 0% (0/55).
results.evaluation: Claims C56-C63 are supported by systematic analysis of coupling rates by cell type shown in Figures 4G-H. The statistical significance (p<0.0001-0.01) and adequate sample sizes support the conclusion that electrical connections preferentially form between same-type neurons, with FFs more likely to connect than MPs.

results.result: FF-FF electrical coupling has higher connection strength (higher coupling coefficients) than MP-MP electrical coupling.
results.evaluation: Claim C64 is supported by comparison of coupling coefficients shown in Figure 4I with statistical significance (p<0.05). This complements the finding of higher FF-FF coupling rates.

results.result: The vast majority of putative electrical synapses form between dendrites (dendro-dendritic), with only two coupled pairs having dendrite-soma synapses and no soma-soma synapses identified, showing no preferential synaptic location for either FF-FF or MP-MP coupled pairs.
results.evaluation: Claims C65-C68 are supported by morphological analysis of coupled pairs shown in Figures 5A-C. The predominance of dendro-dendritic synapses is consistent with prior literature (C129-C130) and the inference about lack of preferential location (C68) is reasonable given the data.

results.result: Putative electrical synapses are located on first or second-order dendritic branches, most frequently in the middle of dendritic trees (average 155 µm from soma), with dendritic distances to the two somata linearly related (r=0.86), and putative synapse number positively correlating with coupling coefficient (r=0.86).
results.evaluation: Claims C69-C72 are supported by morphological measurements shown in Figures 5D-E, G. The correlations (r=0.86 for both) are strong and statistically significant (p<0.01-0.05), supporting the relationship between synapse location/number and coupling strength.

results.result: Multicell recordings demonstrated that electrical signals from one cell hardly pass to other cells via second-order coupling if they are not electrically coupled in the first order, confirming that gap junctions identified with pairwise patch recordings in LC are first-order connections.
results.evaluation: Claims C73 and C138 are supported by experimental observations from multicell recordings (Figure 6A-C example). This is an important validation that addresses a long-standing technical concern about dye-coupling studies (C135-C137).

results.result: In 15 recording sets with more than two electrical connections, coupled pairs often shared the same coupling partner in a chain-like pattern (A↔B↔C), while two coupled pairs without a sharing partner (A↔B, C↔D) were rare, suggesting electrically coupled cells tend to cluster together.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C77 are supported by experimental observations from multicell recordings shown in Figures 6A-D. The inference about chain-like clustering (C77) is reasonable given the observed patterns, though statistical modeling is needed to confirm this is not random.

results.result: For two electrical connections, the observed chain-like pattern (n=16) was higher than predicted by random connectivity model (n=12.9, 95% CI=[6,21]), while non-chain-like patterns (n=5) were significantly less than predicted (n=11.6, 95% CI=[6,19], p=0.01), with observed cluster index of 3.2 significantly higher than Model 1 prediction of 1.1 (p=0.001).
results.evaluation: Claims C78-C80 are supported by statistical modeling comparing observed data to Model 1 predictions (Figures 6D, 7A). The Monte Carlo simulations with 1000 runs provide robust statistical support for the overrepresentation of chain-like patterns.

results.result: Cell-type-specific connectivity rules (Model 2) and additional spatial connectivity rules (Model 3) could not explain the overrepresentation of chain-like patterns, with cluster indices predicted by Models 2 and 3 still significantly lower than observed, suggesting an additional chain-like connectivity rule beyond random, spatial, and cell-type-specific rules.
results.evaluation: Claims C81-C83 are supported by statistical modeling results shown in Figures 7A-B. The systematic testing of increasingly complex models strengthens the conclusion that an additional organizing principle is needed. However, the models assume independence of pairwise connections, which the proposed chain-like rule would violate.

results.result: The most frequent patterns of two electrical connections are FF-FF-FF and MP-MP-MP, while other combinations are rare or absent. For three electrical connections, the chain-like pattern (A↔B↔C↔D) was most frequent, while circular-like and hub cell-like patterns were rarely observed.
results.evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by experimental observations shown in Figures 6D-E. The cell-type specificity of chain patterns is consistent with the homotypic coupling preference, though sample sizes for triple connections are small.

results.result: For three electrical connections, the observed ratio of chain-like to non-chain-like patterns was 2, significantly higher than Model 1 prediction of 0.68±0.25 (p=0.001), with all simulations indicating that an additional chain-like rule may apply beyond spatial and cell-type-specific rules.
results.evaluation: Claims C87-C88 are based on statistical modeling shown in Figure 7B. However, the sample size for triple connections is very small (observed: 2 chain-like, 1 non-chain-like), making the statistical inference less robust than for double connections. The p-value is significant but the confidence intervals are wide, and the authors appropriately use cautious language ('may apply').

results.result: This study represents the first multicell patch recordings of a monoamine modulatory system in the brain, allowing examination of how monoaminergic neurons interact at single-cell level for the first time.
results.evaluation: Claim C89 is a claim about methodological novelty but lacks supporting evidence or citations to verify that no prior multicell recordings of monoamine systems exist. While the technical achievement is impressive, the claim of being 'first' requires more rigorous documentation.

results.result: Noradrenergic neurons in the LC can be classified into at least two major morpho-electric cell types, with neurons within each type forming homotypic network modules via gap junctions that may coordinate their input/output to engage in distinct functions within their efferent domains.
results.evaluation: Claims C90-C91 are well-supported by the experimental data on cell classification and cell-type-specific electrical coupling. Claims C92-C93 about functional implications are more speculative, based on inference from spatial distribution and prior literature about projection targets, but represent reasonable interpretations of the findings.

results.result: Prior studies indicate that the anterior horn and ventral LC core are dominated by multipolar cells that project to spinal cord, cerebellum, and hypothalamus, while the posterior horn and dorsal LC core are dominated by fusiform cells that project to neocortex and hippocampus.
results.evaluation: Claims C94-C96 and C102-C103 are supported by citations to prior research (Loughlin et al., 1986; Swanson, 1976; Waterhouse et al., 1983). This represents established prior knowledge used to interpret the current findings.

results.result: MPs have longer action potentials with smaller amplitude than FFs, and FFs can sustain higher frequency firing than MPs with large suprathreshold depolarizing current injections.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C98 are supported by electrophysiological measurements comparing MP and FF. These represent subtle but significant differences in intrinsic properties between the two cell types.

results.result: While FFs firing narrower spikes suggests they may correspond to 'narrow' units from extracellular recordings and MPs to 'wide' units, there is no consistent evidence supporting this correspondence, with both unit types possibly arising from the same MP type reflecting within-MP functional heterogeneity.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C101 represent speculative discussion about relating the current cell type classification to prior extracellular recording studies. The authors appropriately note inconsistencies (spatial distribution, firing rates, spike width differences) that argue against simple correspondence, but the alternative hypothesis about MP heterogeneity is also speculative.

results.result: FF cells may correspond to fusiform-shaped cells in the posterior horn/dorsal LC core, MP cells may correspond to multipolar cells in the anterior horn/ventral core, and these two types might form separate LC subnetworks with distinct projection domains performing nonoverlapping functions.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C106 are speculative inferences based on morphological similarities to prior anatomical studies. The authors appropriately note difficulty in registering slice recordings to in vivo locations. The functional implications (C106) are reasonable hypotheses but require experimental validation.

results.result: Only a small subset of monoamine neuron terminals may be specialized for glutamate release, and the current results do not rule out that a subset of noradrenergic terminals makes glutamatergic synapses onto other target regions including spinal cord and parabrachial nucleus.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C110 are appropriately cautious interpretations of the negative result for glutamatergic transmission, supported by citations to prior research. This represents reasonable discussion of study limitations.

results.result: NE released from individual LC/NE neurons is not sufficient to activate α2AR to evoke detectable inhibition on LC/NE neurons at least in the in vitro preparation, based on testing more than 1500 cell pairs without detecting hyperpolarization.
results.evaluation: Claim C112 is a reasonable inference from the negative experimental results (C47) testing >1500 pairs. The authors appropriately limit the conclusion to their in vitro preparation and note that other unknown reasons may contribute.

results.result: Recent studies suggest α2AR-mediated lateral inhibition is a frequency-dependent population-wide phenomenon detectable with optogenetic activation of many neurons, and appears to be module-specific rather than nonspecific spatial surround inhibition.
results.evaluation: Claims C113-C114 are supported by citation to a recent study (Davy et al., 2022). This represents prior work that helps explain why single-cell stimulation did not reveal α2AR-mediated effects.

results.result: While several previous studies suggested electrical coupling in LC is negligible or absent in adults and decreases with age, the current multicell recordings provide direct demonstration of electrical coupling in mature LC/NE neurons with coupling rate consistent with prior extracellular recording and comparable to other brain regions.
results.evaluation: Claims C115-C119 represent discussion of how current findings (C116) relate to prior literature. The current data contradict some prior studies (C115, C119) but are consistent with others (C116), representing an important clarification of the field.

results.result: Gap junctions generally form between same-type cells in most brain regions, and LC neurons are intricately connected with close neighboring neurons of the same type to constitute cell-type-specific electrical subnetworks, providing a plausible cellular mechanism for prior observations of cell-type-specific LC pairwise correlated firing and ensembles.
results.evaluation: Claim C121 is supported by citation to prior research. Claims C122-C123 represent well-supported inferences from the experimental data on cell-type-specific coupling, connecting current findings to prior in vivo observations.

results.result: The FF-FF coupling rate is more than threefold higher than MP-MP, suggesting either that MP electrical subnetworks are smaller or that MPs are more heterogeneous, with MP cells in each LC subregion possibly only connecting with MPs in the same subregion to form subregion-specific MP subnetworks.
results.evaluation: Claim C124 is supported by experimental data. Claims C125-C126 are speculative interpretations of the coupling rate difference. The hypothesis about subregion-specific MP subnetworks (C126) is reasonable but requires experimental validation.

results.result: Close appositions identified under light microscopy can be reliably confirmed as electrical synapses by electron microscopy, with more than 50% of electrically coupled LC pairs having only one putative synapse, almost all occurring between dendrites, consistent with dendro-dendritic synapses being the dominant form across brain regions and localizing further from soma with age.
results.evaluation: Claims C127-C131 are supported by citations to prior research and morphological analysis of coupled pairs. The predominance of single dendro-dendritic synapses (C128-C129) is consistent with prior literature (C130-C131).

results.result: Gap junctions at distal dendritic sites can interact locally with chemical synaptic inputs to drive synchronized spiking, either by promoting synchronized response to specific synaptic inputs or by allowing weak distal gap junction inputs to synchronize somatic action potentials upon common chemical synaptic input.
results.evaluation: Claims C132-C134 are supported by citations to prior research. This represents established knowledge about how distal gap junctions can promote synchronization despite small somatic coupling potentials.

results.result: Dye-coupling approaches may provide insight into network organization but neuron clusters could result from second-order coupling that is not discriminable from first-order coupling. Given gap junctions at distal dendrites, somatic membrane potentials are likely highly attenuated by the time they reach post-junctional cells, suggesting gap junctions identified with pairwise recordings should be essentially first-order.
results.evaluation: Claims C135-C137 represent reasonable inferences about technical limitations of dye-coupling approaches and the expected attenuation of signals through dendrodendritic gap junctions. This provides important context for interpreting the multicell recording results.

results.result: A chain-like pattern of two connections (A↔B↔C) is overrepresented in the dataset, and revising models with spatial and cell-type-specific rules did not explain this pattern, suggesting an additional chain-like connectivity rule that may be a general wiring principle dictating whole electrically coupled networks.
results.evaluation: Claims C139-C141 are well-supported by statistical modeling (Figures 6D, 7A-B). Claim C142 about generalization to larger networks is more speculative since no four-connection cases were found, but represents a reasonable hypothesis for future testing.

results.result: Previous dye-based studies suggest chain-like connectivity rules in many brain regions including LC, with dye injection of single cells labeling maximum of two additional cells if only first-order coupled cells are labeled, and the mesencephalic trigeminal nucleus showing gap junctions between five neurons arranged in a chain-like pattern.
results.evaluation: Claims C143-C146 are supported by citations to prior research. This provides important context showing that chain-like organization may be a general principle, though dye-coupling studies have interpretational limitations (C135).
